summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory and no single legal order runs through it. Morocco controls most of the ground, and Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate there; the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims sovereignty and governs through exile institutions and refugee camps in Algeria. What a visitor encounters depends on which part of the territory they are in.

Moroccan jurisdiction reaches into the territory in practice. On 9 December 2005 Human Rights Watch reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The case shows Moroccan courts and detention operating on Sahrawi political cases, not only on paper.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. Moroccan law carries six months to three years of imprisonment. For the SADR, the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both men and women, punishable by up to three years, and a July 2017 PinkNews roundup listed the SADR among jurisdictions where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and had been for decades.

The SADR's own position is contested. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it'. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) reads the same silence as leaving LGBTQ people with no legal protection against discrimination or violence. Constitutional silence is not decriminalisation, and no statute in the inventory decriminalises anything.

The only documented account of the Sahrawi authorities applying such charges comes from a 2009 USCRI report: officials running the refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The charge sits in the hands of camp administration rather than a court.

Social exposure is high. Most residents are Muslim, and same-sex relationships are widely read as a foreign phenomenon. No source in the inventory records a trans-specific statute, a protection mechanism, or a documented case of a trans visitor being processed under either framework.
tangentialFactors:
The legal inheritance runs through two external systems. Western Sahara was under Spanish rule until 1976, and Spain did not decriminalise homosexuality until 1979, so no decriminalising statute was carried into the territory when Spanish administration ended. The provisions in force today derive from Moroccan law in the controlled zone and from the SADR's own framework in the claimed zone.

The two orders are not equally reachable. Morocco's courts, security services and detention facilities operate on the ground. The SADR is partially recognised, has held African Union membership since 2016, and works through exile institutions and the camps in Algeria. A visitor who needs a police report, a court or a consular channel will be dealing with Moroccan institutions across most of the territory.

Neither order supplies a protection mechanism. CEAR's reading of the SADR Constitution leaves LGBTQ people without recourse against discrimination or violence, and no source in the inventory records a hate-crime provision, an anti-discrimination clause or a trans-specific protection in either framework.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Sahrawi-run refugee camps in Algeria carry the sharpest documented exposure. The 2009 USCRI report found that camp officials said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape, which places the charge in the hands of camp administration rather than a court.

CEAR states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. It reaches that conclusion from the SADR Constitution's silence on sexual practice, which the SADR's 2010 diplomatic representative in Mexico, Ahmed Mulay Alli, presented as evidence that the constitution does not punish it.

Organised rights work carries its own risk. Seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara stood trial in 2005 on charges of fomenting illegal protests that Human Rights Watch called dubious, and the prosecution ran through Moroccan courts.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a trans-specific statute, a gender-marker or identity-document rule, a facilities provision, or an entry rule for Western Sahara. The visitor assessment rests on the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and on the absence of protection machinery, not on documented treatment of trans travellers as a distinct category.

The criminalisation attributed to the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic is recorded by secondary compilations, a 2017 news roundup and the ILGA, Equaldex and Council for Global Equality summaries, rather than by a cited statutory text. The 2010 statement by the SADR's representative in Mexico is the only official characterisation in the inventory and it denies punishment, while CEAR reads the same silence as leaving conduct unprotected. Which reading governs in practice is unresolved.

The 2009 USCRI account of detentions on 'homosexuality' charges is second-hand, resting on statements by camp officials who described the underlying facts as rape. No prosecution figures and no trans-specific violence data with a denominator appear in the inventory.

The most recent enforcement documentation in the inventory is the 2005 Human Rights Watch dispatch. Enforcement in the Moroccan-controlled part since then is not sourced here.
